What Code-Fix read in the source and proposed, in Code-Fix's words - nothing ran its test or its fix, and what it claims is not what happened unless a row of the record shows it:
  - [F1] The fault (in main's src/io_shop/spend_summary.py): `average_spend_per_item_this_month` builds the list of purchases with `in_current_month` set and divides `account.total_this_month_cents` by the length of that list. A shopper who has bought before but not this month has an empty list, so the division raises ZeroDivisionError. That is an ordinary shopper, not an edge case: the existing test helper `an_account_with_no_purchases_this_month` calls it "the ordinary case". `render_spend_summary` reaches this function whenever `use_monthly_summary` is true and `use_typical_spend` is false. In src/io_shop/account_page.py, `serve_account_page` calls it through `_the_figure_for`, which does so when no cache is configured or the cache returns nothing. The exception then reaches the boundary's broad `except`, and the whole page fails, not just the figure. So switching the monthly rollout on failed every idle shopper who fell into its slice. When the flag is off the lifetime path runs, which hid the problem without fixing it.
      
      The fix: when nothing was bought this month, the function now returns 0 {F1.1}. That is the true answer, not a guess: the shopper spent nothing this month, which is what `total_this_month_cents` already says for such an account. Every other case goes through the same floor division as before. The lifetime average, the typical-spend path and the flag-off path are unchanged. A shopper with no history at all still raises on the lifetime path, and the existing test `test_the_page_lets_a_failure_reach_its_caller` pins that, so nothing is silenced. Only the case that was never a failure now gets a figure. The function's signature and return type stay the same, so `render_spend_summary` and its callers in account_page.py need no change.
      
      Tests (tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py): two new cases are written to show that, with the monthly path selected, an account with past purchases but none this month gets 0 {F1.2}, both from the function directly and from `render_spend_summary(..., use_monthly_summary=True)`. Against the current code both would raise ZeroDivisionError.
      
      About revisions: everything above describes main. The revision that ran, 383534e9…, is not in main's history and I have not read it, so I can't confirm that its code at this line is the same. Two more notes on main. First, src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py's docstring says `monthly-spend-feature` gates the statement panel. Second, `render_monthly_statement` there calls `max`/`min` over the month's purchases before its own mean division, so for an empty month it would raise ValueError, not ZeroDivisionError. Its docstring says that raise is deliberate, and I have left it alone. So the ZeroDivisionError the investigation names matches the spend-summary path fixed here. If the flag also gates the statement in production, idle shoppers would still hit that documented ValueError there. That is a separate decision for whoever owns the panel.
  - Say what the files Code-Fix read do, with the conditions it gives - a default as a default, never as all it does - and no wider: 'nothing in the files it read', never 'nothing in the code'. [F1] was written against main, which does not contain the revision running when the alert fired: merged, its fix changes what runs only once a deploy carries it. [F1] names tests/io_shop/test_spend_summary.py, src/io_shop/monthly_statement.py on main as they were at 383534e, which ran. What [F1] says of those files holds for what ran; what it says of the rest of main does not. [F1] names revision 383534e9 and [D1] is that revision's own diff - say what it shows rather than ask for it to be checked.

      """Serving one account page - the shop's request boundary.
      
      This is the line at which an exception stops being a bug and becomes an
      incident: everything below it raises, and here it is caught, recorded in the
      shop's own words, and turned into a failed response. It is the only place in the
      shop that catches broadly, and it does so on purpose - a request handler that let
      an unexpected error escape would take the worker with it instead of reporting a
      rate somebody can alert on.
      """
      
      from __future__ import annotations
      
      import traceback
      from dataclasses import dataclass
      from pathlib import PurePath
      
      from io_shop.accounts import Account
      from io_shop.monthly_statement import (
          MonthlyStatement,
          StatementPeriod,
          render_monthly_statement,
      )
      from io_shop.payment_provider import AskTheProvider, card_on_file
      from io_shop.pricing_service import AskThePricingService, basket_total
      from io_shop.spend_summary import render_spend_summary
      from io_shop.summary_cache import (
          CacheEndpoint,
          CacheUnreachable,
          LookUpSummary,
          cached_summary,
      )
      from io_shop.visits import record_visit
      
      
      @dataclass(frozen=True)
      class RenderedPage:
          """How serving one account page went.
      
          Either the page rendered, in which case both of the things it shows are
          here, or it failed, in which case neither is and `failure` carries the
          error's own words and the line they were raised on - because those are what
          reach the log and what a reader diagnoses from. A generic "request failed"
          would describe every incident equally, and the error's words alone name a
          fault without naming where it lives.
      
          `statement` is the monthly statement panel, on the pages the newest rollout
          reached and absent everywhere else. It sits beside the figure rather than
          replacing it: the statement is a second thing the page shows, so a request
          outside the rollout renders the page it always rendered rather than a
          shorter one.
      
          `served_from_cache` says whether the figure was read rather than worked out.
          It is reported on a page that rendered perfectly well, because it is the
          difference between the two ways of rendering perfectly well - and the share
          of requests taking each is what says whether the shop's fast path is there.
      
          `cache_failure` carries the words of a cache that could not be reached. It
          sits beside `failure` rather than in it, and the distinction is the whole
          scenario: this is a page that *succeeded* while something underneath it was
          broken, so a reader sees it in the logs without seeing it in the error rate.
      
          `pricing_delay` is the same shape of thing for the same reason: the words of
          a pricing call that took longer than the shop thinks worth passing over. The
          page was correct and the shopper was charged the right amount; what a reader
          gets from this line is where the request's time went, which is the one thing
          no amount of the shop's own telemetry can say.
          """
      
          figure_cents: int | None
          card_last_four: str | None
          failure: str | None
          served_from_cache: bool = False
          cache_failure: str | None = None
          statement: MonthlyStatement | None = None
          basket_total_cents: int | None = None
          pricing_delay: str | None = None
      
      
      def serve_account_page(account: Account,
                             use_monthly_summary: bool,
                             ask_the_provider: AskTheProvider,
                             ask_the_pricing_service: AskThePricingService,
                             look_up_summary: LookUpSummary | None = None,
                             cache_endpoint: CacheEndpoint | None = None,
                             use_typical_spend: bool = False,
                             use_monthly_statement: bool = False,
                             statement_period: StatementPeriod | None = None
                             ) -> RenderedPage:
          """Renders the account page, reporting a failure rather than raising one.
      
          Three things are shown and all three are needed: what the shopper averages
          per item, which Io works out for itself; what their basket comes to, which
          the pricing service works out; and the card it would charge, which only the
          payment provider knows. The last two are calls to other services from inside
          a page render, which is ordinary and is why a slowdown or an outage over
          there arrives here as Io's own latency and Io's own error rate.
      
          The two are not the same kind of neighbour, and nothing in this function
          tells them apart: one is another team's service and one is another company's,
          and which is which is published in the service catalogue rather than
          inferred from a host name.
      
          `use_monthly_summary` and `use_typical_spend` are the rollout decisions
          already made - whether this request is one of the ones each new figure is
          live for. The page does not make those decisions itself; it is told, the way
          a handler is told by the flag SDK that evaluated for this user. Two of them
          because there are two rollouts running, and a page carrying one boolean for
          both would be a page that cannot say which feature a request got.
      
          `look_up_summary` and `cache_endpoint` are how the figure is looked for
          before it is worked out. Both optional and both absent together, because a
          deployment that configured no cache has none - and a page that insisted on
          one would make an optimisation into a requirement, which is the very thing
          this shop's cache is not.
      
          `use_monthly_statement` is the third rollout decision, and it arrives here
          already made like the other two. `statement_period` is which month the
          request is asking about, which the page is told rather than deriving: the
          shop's purchase records carry a month flag and no date, so the only thing
          here that knows the calendar is whoever handled the request.
          """
          try:
              figure_cents, from_cache, cache_failure = _the_figure_for(
                  account, use_monthly_summary, look_up_summary, cache_endpoint,
                  use_typical_spend
              )
              statement = _the_statement_for(
                  account, use_monthly_statement, statement_period
              )
              basket = basket_total(account.shopper_id, ask_the_pricing_service)
              card = card_on_file(account.shopper_id, ask_the_provider)
          except Exception as error:  # noqa: BLE001 - the boundary records anything
              failure = f"{type(error).__name__}: {error} at {_where_it_was_raised(error)}"
              record_visit(account.shopper_id, failure)
      
              return RenderedPage(figure_cents=None, card_last_four=None, failure=failure)
      
          record_visit(account.shopper_id, str(figure_cents))
      
          return RenderedPage(figure_cents=figure_cents,
                              card_last_four=card.last_four,
                              failure=None,
                              served_from_cache=from_cache,
                              cache_failure=cache_failure,
                              statement=statement,
                              basket_total_cents=basket.total_cents,
                              pricing_delay=basket.slow_call)
      
      
      def _the_statement_for(account: Account,
                             use_monthly_statement: bool,
                             period: StatementPeriod | None) -> MonthlyStatement | None:
          """The monthly statement panel, where this request is one the rollout
          reached, and nothing where it is not.
      
          Nothing also where the request arrived without a period. That is a
          misconfigured caller rather than a shopper's month, and rendering a
          statement titled with a month nobody named would put a wrong heading over
          correct figures - see `io_shop.monthly_statement.StatementPeriod`, which is
          where that argument is made at length. A missing panel is visible to
          whoever configured the rollout; a wrongly titled one is visible only to the
          shopper.
          """
          if not use_monthly_statement or period is None:
              return None
      
          return render_monthly_statement(account, period)
      
      
      def _the_figure_for(
          account: Account,
          use_monthly_summary: bool,
          look_up_summary: LookUpSummary | None,
          cache_endpoint: CacheEndpoint | None,
          use_typical_spend: bool
      ) -> tuple[int, bool, str | None]:
          """The figure to show, whether it came from the cache, and what the cache
          said if it could not be reached.
      
          The cache is asked first and is allowed to fail. Whatever it does - answers
          with a figure, answers with nothing, or cannot be reached at all - this
          returns a figure, because the shop can always work one out. That is the
          fallback the whole scenario rests on: the page is correct either way, and
          the only thing the cache decides is how long getting here took.
      
          A cache failure is returned rather than raised onward, because it is not
          this request's failure. The request succeeded.
          """
          if look_up_summary is None or cache_endpoint is None:
              return render_spend_summary(
                  account,
                  use_monthly_summary=use_monthly_summary,
                  use_typical_spend=use_typical_spend
              ), False, None
      
          cache_failure: str | None = None
      
          try:
              found = cached_summary(account.shopper_id, look_up_summary, cache_endpoint)

  - [S2] src/io_shop/spend_summary.py at 383534e
      """What a shopper has spent, and what that averages to.
      
      Three figures about one history. The lifetime average has been on the account
      page for years; the monthly one narrows it to the current month; the typical
      purchase abandons the average altogether for the middle of the history. The
      last two are the ones still behind a rollout, and which of them a request gets
      is decided before it reaches here.
      """
      
      from __future__ import annotations
      
      from datetime import UTC, datetime
      
      from io_shop.accounts import Account
      from io_shop.typical_spend import typical_spend_per_item
      
      
      def average_spend_per_item(account: Account) -> int:
          """Average spend per item across everything this account has ever bought.
      
          Live for years. Its divisor is empty only for an account that has never
          bought anything at all, which no real shopper is.
      
          Derives the total from the purchases rather than reading the one the account
          carries, taking each purchase in and recomputing what has been spent by
          then, so that the figure agrees with the list the shopper is looking at even
          where the totals the query returned have drifted from it.
          """
          spent_by_then = 0 {S2.1}
      
          for index, _ in enumerate(account.purchases):
              spent_by_then = sum(
                  earlier.price_cents for earlier in account.purchases[:index + 1 {S2.2}]
              )
      
          return spent_by_then // len(account.purchases)
      
      
      def average_spend_per_item_this_month(account: Account) -> int:
          """Average spend per item this month.
      
          Narrows the lifetime figure to the current month, so the account page can
          show what a shopper is spending now rather than what they averaged over
          three years.
      
          This month is decided from when the purchase was recorded rather than from
          the flag the writer set, so that a record which sat in a queue over a month
          boundary counts against the month it happened in.
          """
          now = datetime.now(UTC)
          bought_this_month = [
              purchase
              for purchase in account.purchases
              if purchase.recorded_at is not None
              and purchase.recorded_at.month == now.month
              and purchase.recorded_at.year == now.year
          ]
          return account.total_this_month_cents // len(bought_this_month)
      
      
      def render_spend_summary(account: Account,
                               use_monthly_summary: bool,
                               use_typical_spend: bool = False) -> int:
          """The figure Io's account page shows, through whichever version the rollout
          selects.
      
          Raises whatever the selected version raises. Catching belongs at the request
          boundary - see `io_shop.account_page` - where there is a response to turn a
          failure into and a log to record it in. A page that swallowed its own errors
          would render a wrong number instead of an error, which is a worse incident
          than the one it hid.
      
          Two rollouts, so two flags to be told about, and the newer one wins where a
          request is inside both. That is the ordinary arrangement: each is a slice of
          traffic, the slices overlap, and the page has to render one figure.
          """
          if use_typical_spend:
              return typical_spend_per_item(account)
      
          if use_monthly_summary:
              return average_spend_per_item_this_month(account)
      
          return average_spend_per_item(account)
      

Action items the record already holds:
  - AI-1 (mitigate, done): Reverted the feature flag monthly-spend-feature
  - AI-2 (prevent, open): Review and merge the proposed fix
PR #413 is a draft Argus opened for a person to review and merge. The record holds nothing about it after that: do not say it was reviewed, approved or merged, or that it was not - nor that the record holds nothing, which the document says itself. Nothing ran its test or its fix: say what it proposes, not that it corrects anything.
The document already states what set it off, in a section of its own: the change [P3].

Cite evidence in causal_chain by its label. In a contributing factor's addressed_by, name the record's own action items that answer it, by their number; an item you propose names the factors it answers in its answers, by their labels.

Call submit_postmortem with your answer.

action_items.item: Make CI run the account-page tests with each rollout flag switched on, including an account with past purchases but none this month, so that a change to code behind a flag is tested on the path the flag selects.
Find out how revision 383534e came to be deployed to production when Code-Fix found it not in main's history, and whether it passed review.
Ramp io-shop feature flags up in steps, checking the error rate between steps, instead of switching them on for most traffic at once.
Do not switch on a flag in the same minute as a deploy that changes the code it gates: wait until the deploy is seen healthy with the flag off.
Once the fix is merged, deploy a revision carrying it to io-shop in place of revision 383534e. The recorded_at change in 383534e is not in main, so its owner must decide whether it ships.

Before monthly-spend-feature is switched back on, have the statement panel's owner decide whether render_monthly_statement should still raise for an empty month. Code-Fix read it as raising ValueError there and found the flag named as gating that panel.
Link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call page so that a person is brought in.
Find out why the deployment platform's API server was unavailable, and restore it so that rollbacks of io-shop can be done.

causal_chain.step: Some shoppers' account page requests failed. Account-page error warnings rose above their usual level, and the error rate the alert watches (the share of all the service's requests answered with a server error) stayed above its threshold until the alert fired.

Those requests raised ZeroDivisionError in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py. The account page's request boundary catches any exception and returns a failed page, so the whole page failed and not just one figure.

ruled_out.what: The earlier deploy of revision 65279ee at {P1.1}: the metrics read across the hours before the onset show the service at its usual error rate with that revision in place. Account pages were logged rendering normally, and the flag was logged off, up to the onset.

Revision 383534e, deployed at {P2.1}, breaking pages without the flag: after the flag was switched off, the service left the incident's level and the revert was confirmed. The rollback of that revision was never done, so it was still running when the service recovered.

causal_chain.step: Requests reached the monthly spend average in spend_summary.py because the feature flag monthly-spend-feature was switched on at {P3.1}. From {G971b.6} most of the flag's evaluations came back on, and from {Gce95.4} every evaluation logged was on. When a request's monthly-summary rollout decision is on, render_spend_summary sends it to average_spend_per_item_this_month.

The monthly average failed for shoppers with no purchase recorded this month because revision 383534e had removed its empty-month guard. That revision was deployed at {P2.1}, and at {T10.1} it was running on every replica.

input.cause_in_plain_words: A code change removed the step that handled shoppers who had bought nothing this month, and when a new feature that uses that code was switched on, the account page failed for those shoppers.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that caught the removal of the empty-month guard before revision 383534e was deployed. By Code-Fix's reading of the test file, no existing test ran the monthly path for an account with past purchases but none this month.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test running the monthly path for a shopper with no purchases this month would have failed on that revision, and it would not have reached production in that form.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: The flag was switched on for most traffic at once, at the same instant as the deploy that changed the code it gates, with no gradual ramp seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Exposing the new code to a small slice first would have limited the failures to that slice and shown the error rise before most shoppers were reached.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

got_lucky: The faulty code was reached only through a flag, which Argus could switch off through the flag provider while the deployment platform was unreachable. The pages recovered without a rollback.

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent read the diff of the deploy that landed at the onset, which shows the empty-month guard removed.
Argus moved on to the flag candidate C2 when the rollback for C1 could not be done.
The Mitigation Agent switched monthly-spend-feature off. The action can be put back.
The Mitigation Agent watched the service leave the incident's level and judged the revert confirmed.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix as a draft pull request for a person to review.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: the alert was linked to no on-call incident, so no person was brought in, even when the rollback could not be done.
The rollback of revision 383534e could not be done because the deployment platform's API answered {T19.2}, so the revision without the guard was left running.

input.root_cause: Revision 383534e removed from average_spend_per_item_this_month the guard that returned {D1.1} for a shopper who had bought nothing this month, and changed it to count only purchases whose recorded_at falls in the current month. For any shopper with no such purchase, it now floor-divides total_this_month_cents by the length of an empty list and raises ZeroDivisionError. The account page's request boundary catches that error and fails the whole page.
input.still_at_risk: While revision 383534e stays running, switching monthly-spend-feature back on would fail account pages again for shoppers with no purchase recorded this month.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for some shoppers

system.text:
You write the postmortem for an incident Argus has already handled. One message describes it - what Argus did and read, the candidate causes, the actions and what they came to, and every figure already measured - and you answer by calling submit_postmortem. Nothing is left to look up.

The candidates are the Investigator's account, written while the incident ran and before anything was tried. The record - the lines saying what Argus did, the changes, the log lines, the actions and their verdicts - is what happened. Where the two disagree, the record is right.

Write causal_chain as the five whys. The first step is the symptom: what the people using the service saw, with the evidence that shows it. The symptom field is that step in a few words, and the two must agree. Each step after it answers why the step before happened - one cause, no jumps - and cites its evidence from the record, never a candidate: a candidate is a hypothesis, and the chain says what happened. Five is a guide, not a quota: stop where the evidence stops. The root_cause field says the mechanism: the step of the chain that says why the change broke the service.

A why the record cannot answer - a missing test, a missing safeguard, an alert that came late - is a contributing factor rather than a step, and each contributing factor names an action item that answers it. Where one why has several answers, follow the one that leads to the fault and make the others contributing factors.

Never stop at a person. Where somebody's action set the incident off, ask why the system let that action do harm - why it was possible at all - and carry on from there.

tools.description: Submit the postmortem for this incident. Every field is required. Write no figure yourself anywhere in your answer - no time, duration, percentage, count or amount, not in digits and not spelled out in words. Every figure you are shown is followed by its name in braces, like {A3} or {duration}: where your prose states one, write its name, braces and all, and the document writes the figure in. A figure you were not shown but could work out from two you were - the span between two instants, how far one share is above another, how many times one is the other - is written as that working, braces and all: {back_to_normal - began}, {T3.1 - alert_raised}, {errors_at_worst / errors_before}. The document works it out from the figures as you were shown them. Say any other size with no number in it, not even in a word - "most requests", "for several minutes", never "twenty minutes", "a third" or "tripled". A number is a figure even with a unit or a clock's marks on it (5m, 10ms, 3x, 12:05Z). Any other word with a digit in it is a name - a label (T2, G3fa2, C1, AI-1), a version (v2), a revision, a pod - and is written as given. State only what the evidence you are shown says: where the record does not show something - a check that was or was not run, how many replicas - leave it out or say it was not seen.

action_items.description: What should be done that the record does not already hold, each one thing a person could take on: two things to do are two items. Empty where the record's own items answer every factor. Propose nothing to confirm a cause the record already confirmed - a mitigation that worked, a hypothesis marked confirmed - and no check of what the evidence you are shown already shows: a diff states what changed. Where an F row says to check something a D row shows, say what the D row shows, and the item is what follows from it. Where Code-Fix proposed a fix, propose no item to run or check its reading: where the cause rests on it, the review checklist says what would confirm it, under the record's own item for the fix.

answers.description: The labels of the contributing factors it answers: CF-1. Empty where it answers none.

assumptions.description: Anything else the reader should know was assumed rather than measured. Empty is a valid answer.

causal_chain.description: The cause as the five whys, from the symptom down: the first step is what users saw - or, where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, that and what was seen instead - and each step after it answers why the step directly before it happened. The first why says why the symptom happened, not the symptom again in more detail. Where the record holds them, the document says itself how bad it got, which change set it off, what put the service back and the root cause: a step cites the row that shows one of those and does not say it again - no figure the impact gives in the first step, no action Argus took, nor its verdict, in the step naming the change, and, where the chain says why the change broke the service, its last step says that in one sentence, its mechanism left to the root cause. Where the incident needed two things at once - something going wrong, and nothing in place to contain it - follow the one that leads to what set it off; the other is one of the contributing_factors, not named in the chain. A safeguard that did not stop it is never a step of its own: it is one of the contributing_factors. Every step cites at least one piece of evidence by its label. Date a change by its own row's instant - the T or P row that records it - never by an effect it had. A state a row read - how many replicas run a revision, which way a flag is set - is known as of the row that read it, by that row's instant, which is its first figure, as T3.1 is T3's - not from when the change was made. What else the record ruled out - an earlier change, a flag the provider showed unchanged, a candidate refuted - goes in the ruled_out of the step that ties the incident to the change that set it off, citing what ruled it out, and never as a step. An earlier change is ruled out only by the service measured healthy with it in place - in metrics read between it and the onset, in an alert that dates the first harm itself at or after a later change (at, where the two instants are the same), or after a confirmed action that left it there - never by how long before the onset it came. Where the record shows none of these, it was not ruled out: say so in that step itself. Stop where the evidence stops.

cites.description: The labels of the evidence that shows this step: T3, G3fa2. Not rows that merely happened at the same time.

ruled_out.description: What else the record ruled out at this step, each what it was and why. Empty on every step but the one that ties the incident to the change that set it off.

cites.description: The labels of what ruled it out.

cause_in_plain_words.description: What caused the incident, in one sentence for a reader who does not work on the service: no component names unless they are unavoidable. When it began, for how long, how bad it got, what customers lost and what was done the document says itself - say none of them. Say only what the record says - of a change, of the service, of the people - and nothing it does not. Where part of it rests only on a reading nothing ran, say that part as likely, in plain words, without mentioning the reading.

cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading.description: Whether the mechanism in root_cause rests on an F row - a reading of the code nothing ran - with no S or D row showing what it rests on. Where you answer true, the document says itself, beside the root cause, that the cause is unverified, and leaves its root-cause review box for a person: say neither in root_cause.

contributing_factors.description: Conditions that had to hold for the incident to happen and did not cause it alone - a safeguard that did not stop it, a gap in detection or review. A factor held before the incident began: what the response did, declined or left behind - an action taken or not, automatic sync left off - is not one; where it went wrong, say it under went_wrong. Not the root cause again in other words: a factor is something that, had it been otherwise, would have stopped or shortened the incident even with what root_cause says still true. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. An alert finds what its rule watches, not the cause behind it: say a fault was found only by what the record shows found it. Each is answered by at least one action item: one of the record's, named in its addressed_by, or one you propose, whose answers name it.

addressed_by.description: The record's own action items that answer it, by the numbers the record gives them: AI-1. Empty where none of them does. Never an item you propose: that item names, in its own answers, the factors it answers. The record's item that merges this incident's fix answers the fault its own tests cover, never a check missing before the change went out: answer that with an item that puts the check in place for every change like it.

had_it_been_otherwise.description: What would have gone differently had this been otherwise - stopped, shortened or caught sooner - with what root_cause says still true. A factor that only says the root cause again cannot answer this: leave it out of the list.

label.description: CF-1 for the first factor, CF-2 for the next, and so on in the order you give them. Written here and in an item's answers, never in your prose: the reader never sees it.

lessons.description: What went well, what went wrong, and where the incident got lucky - a risk that went unnoticed this time. Any list may be empty. A safeguard the record does not show is one not seen, never one absent: write that no check was seen, not that none ran. How soon the alert came is weighed by the document already, from what was measured: say nothing of it here.

got_lucky.description: Something the record shows went the fortunate way by chance, and how it kept the harm down - never what would have happened otherwise. Empty where the record shows none. Not what kind of fault it was, which the impact already says, nor a limit of what the record shows, which is said in assumptions as what was assumed. Not how the service did over a stretch its metrics did not cover, nor what a failure there would have done - the document says how it did.

went_well.description: Only what went well; empty where nothing did. A timed item says one thing, done at its row; what came later goes in an item of its own. Say no span of time, in figures or in words ("within seconds"): name the row in timed_by instead, and begin an item timed so with who did it ("The Investigator Agent ...", "Argus ..."), since the document says the time ahead of it. Set a purpose or a reason beside the action it belongs to, and say it once. Name what Code-Fix proposed without saying what it does: the action items and Code-Fix's own reading say that, with its conditions.

timed_by.description: The T or XW row the item happened on (T13), where when it happened is part of why it went well: the document says how long after the alert that was. Left out where its time is not the point.

went_wrong.description: A change the response left in place on purpose, which one of the record's own action items undoes (automatic sync left off), went as designed and did not go wrong; so did what the design leaves to a person - a draft fix to review and merge. Not a limit of what the record shows - logs nobody read, metrics that stop short of the onset: the document says what was read, and anything assumed is said in assumptions. Not the root cause or a contributing factor again - the document says those already. Not that Code-Fix read another revision than the one that ran, or that nothing ran its reading: where the record holds them, the document says the first in its summary and the second beside the root cause.

reaches_a_cause.description: Whether the chain says why the change that set the incident off broke the service, rather than stopping at that change. A step resting on F rows - a reading of the code nothing ran - counts: whether that leaves the cause unverified is cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading's to say. That a new version does worse is what the change did, not why it broke the service: answer false where the chain says the evidence does not show why.

root_cause.description: What caused the incident, in one or two sentences, written for an engineer who was not on the call: the mechanism - why the change that set it off broke the service, as far as the evidence goes, a missing protection or not. Not the trigger, how it was confirmed, what resolved it or what was ruled out - the document states each of those itself. Not one of the contributing_factors: a safeguard that would have stopped it with this mechanism unchanged is said there, not here. What the service did over the stretch the metrics did not watch is not the mechanism: the document says it itself. Whether it was verified the document says itself, from your answer to cause_rests_on_an_unrun_reading - do not say it.

still_at_risk.description: What was still at risk at the end of the time Argus held the incident, in one sentence for the same reader - what the fault still in place then could yet do, or the same thing able to happen again. Empty where nothing was. Not whether the service or its metrics were back, nor why - the summary says both. Not what Argus left to a person - a draft fix, automatic sync left off, a recommended action - which the document says itself. Say what could happen, never why it would: no "because". The summary says the cause, or that none was found. Say only what the record says: nothing of the service after that was read.

symptom.description: What went wrong as somebody using the service saw it, as short as it can be: it is the document's title. One sentence with no number in it, never over 16 words - the thing that went wrong and what happened to it, with an active verb: 'Account pages failed'. Not the metric the alert fired on, not the cause - the document adds the change it began with itself, after your sentence and a 'while', so end on what went wrong, with no clause after it - and not how it was found, which the document's Detection says. Where nobody using the service saw anything wrong, say that and what was seen instead, in that one sentence.
